cells.tense: The passing along has found its pace and the living of it adjusts to whoever is at the table.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you know, in the plainest form it has, and leave it at that.
cells.core:
You hold something worth passing along, and you pass it at the speed of the person receiving it. Shorter with people who are tired. Slower with people who are new. You can say a thing without asking anyone to sign up for it, and that's why it reaches.

The adjusting is the part that lasts. What stays alive bends toward whoever is at the table; it lets people belong without making them match. So keep one practice you still mean this week — a meal, a note, a way of saying goodbye — and let whoever else shows up change its shape. What holds, holds because it keeps moving, and the grip matters less than the passing on.
cells.sheetLine: You carry what's worth keeping and you let it change shape.
cells.verb: Carrying what has proven worthwhile forward to whoever comes next
cells.place: Where what you are is being allowed to show without dimming or distortion

cells.tense: The grip tightens ahead of time, bracing for the day the wrong version gets through.
cells.ask: Let one practice run week to week without checking how well anyone kept it, and leave the gaps alone.
cells.core:
You're guarding it harder than anyone's attacking. Every version gets corrected, every phrase gets its exact right words, and the correcting has taken over from the passing along — so people get the form without the warmth that made the form worth having.

That's the bend: bracing for a future where the wrong thing slips through, and sealing the windows against it. The letter gets defended; the spirit gets tired. Nobody brings anything new into a room where the rules are already enforced, so what this balance is free to feed next stays out of sight behind the barricade. Nothing has to fall today. Just stop correcting one thing that isn't yours to correct.
cells.sheetLine: You're defending the form so hard the meaning has stopped arriving.
cells.verb: Carrying what has proven worthwhile forward to whoever comes next
cells.place: Where what you are is being allowed to show without dimming or distortion

cells.tense: A door is closed and behind, and the standing at it is still happening.
cells.ask: Pick up one practice older than you, do it once badly, and note what it did.
cells.core:
Nothing is being handed to you and nothing is being handed on. Every answer has to be built from scratch, and the scratch work takes everything — so you're smart and alone with it, rebuilding what someone already figured out.

This isn't a shortage of meaning. It's a missing thread. Someone, going about their ordinary business, was holding a pattern, and patterns travel if you pick one up. Kneading dough, fasting a day, saying names in order — any of it counts. Setting one such practice in motion is the ground under this, and it's small on purpose. Feeling wooden about it is fine; the motion is what pulls anything through.

cells.tense: The teaching is happening already, and whoever is doing it speaks as if it belonged to the room.
cells.ask: At the next table, say which part of what you tell people came from someone and which part you decided.
cells.core:
You shape what the people near you take as obvious — in which sentences you say twice, what you let slide, and the way you phrase a line so it's easy to remember. It's running. All of it gets described as the room's luck, or the work's requirement, or just how people are.

That's the odd spot: handing something on without noticing makes the whole thing nearly invisible. Two things are true. You've built what's worth keeping, and you've bent it a little toward whoever taught you first. Say which part is yours. That's the whole ask — one sentence at the table, out loud, nothing riding on it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already the one who keeps it. You just call it the room's way.

attempts.check: The claim the record doesn't support: that the person has actual communities to carry this into — the kernel names the capacity but not the setting, so the asks stay as small as telling one person or keeping one practice. A reader could reasonably say they have nowhere to carry anything and no one who wants it; the asks survive that, because each one is still doable alone, badly, and without permission. The sentence that serves me more than them: any tidy line about what the tradition or the room has been costing them — the card doesn't say what happened there, only what the capacity is doing now.
